episodes.title: Anthropic's Record IPO + What Kevin Got Wrong About the Company in 2023
episodes.about: Anthropic is officially a publicly traded company worth more than a trillion dollars, but some of the people getting rich aren't celebrating. We unpack how employees and early investors are reacting and what the debut tells us about the AI bubble. Then we open up our reporter's notebooks from 2023, when Anthropic was just a 150-person lab with a cramped office, bragging about having "hundreds" of customers. We talk about how this strange company got to this moment and how to feel about the biggest IPO in history going to a company that warns its technology could lead to catastrophe. And finally, we open Pandora's Box: Jensen Huang wants his job back, Tesla will sell you a Cybercab (with strings attached), and the kids might actually be all right.
episodes.why: Roose and Newton unpack Anthropic's first day as a public company worth over a trillion dollars and what the debut says about the AI bubble, then open their 2023 notebooks from when Anthropic was a 150-person lab warning its own technology could lead to catastrophe.

episodes.title: Why You Should Try Gemini Neon (Even if You Love Fable)
episodes.about: Google's Gemini Neon edged out Fable on a coding benchmark, but its best pitch may be as a second opinion. NLW shares how Neon helped him find the story in an oil episode that Claude and ChatGPT kept turning into a Wikipedia entry, and what happened when he pushed back on its ideas. In the headlines: Anthropic closes its first day of trading up 17%, and Chinese AI labs warn that new U.S. chip restrictions could delay model releases.
episodes.why: Gemini Neon edged out Fable on a coding benchmark, but NLW's case is to use it as a second opinion: it found the story in an oil episode that Claude and ChatGPT kept flattening into a Wikipedia entry, and held up when he pushed back on its ideas.

episodes.title: Why the Agent Era Needs a New Operating System | DHH
episodes.about: David Heinemeier Hansson thinks the agent era is reopening a window in computing that has been closed for decades: the chance to build a new operating system people actually want to use. DHH joins a16z General Partners Martin Casado and Anish Acharya to explain why he's building Omarchy, an agent-first Linux distribution designed around a computer that users can modify simply by asking. They discuss why the command lines, config files, and detailed error messages that once made Linux intimidating now make it unusually well suited to agents, and why DHH believes software development has become cheap enough to challenge decades-old platform lock-in. But if code is becoming abundant, what still matters? DHH argues that taste, craft, and the willingness to obsess over the final 2% become more important, not less.
episodes.why: DHH argues agents reopen a window closed for decades: a new operating system people actually want. He's building Omarchy, an agent-first Linux distro you modify by asking, because the command lines and error messages that made Linux intimidating now suit agents better than GUIs.

episodes.title: Are You Planning 20,000 AI Agents? Capital One Has a Warning | Abhijit Bose
episodes.about: Most enterprises are still trying to figure out how to get a handful of AI agents into production. Capital One is running tens of thousands. Abhijit Bose, Senior VP and leader of the company's AI/ML platform engineering organization, joins Craig Smith to explain how a decade-old bet on the cloud became the foundation for everything Capital One is doing in AI today, from proprietary GPU clusters built in a single quarter to a platform that took model deployment from months down to about a week. The conversation gets concrete: a 24/7 AI concierge now running across car dealership websites, a generative AI system serving all 20,000-plus of Capital One's call center agents, and the Macau framework, Capital One's answer to the governance problem that's keeping most regulated industries from putting agentic AI into production. Bose's closing argument: deploying five agents is manageable without a platform; deploying 20,000 is a different problem entirely.
episodes.why: Capital One runs tens of thousands of agents while most companies are stuck on a handful; Bose explains the decade-old cloud bet behind it, the concierge running on dealership sites, and why deploying 20,000 agents is a different problem from deploying five.

episodes.title: Julian Gewirtz on the AI risks that actually scare Beijing
episodes.about: What would it take for Beijing to take AI risk seriously, and what could a US-China deal on AI realistically look like? Julian Gewirtz, historian and former senior director for China and Taiwan affairs at the National Security Council under President Biden, argues that any answer has to "start with the reality of what China is and what the Chinese Communist Party cares about." The Party's top concern is regime security, so when Chinese discourse warns of "extreme loss-of-control risks," it means losing political control as well as losing control of AI systems. In Julian's view, what is most likely to shift Beijing's approach to AI safety is China's "own domestic sense of the risks." Next is seeing the US regulate AI at home: a "costly signal" that Washington takes the risks seriously. He says Anthropic's Claude Mythos has been the most significant event shaping Beijing's thinking on AI risk over the past year, sharpening its longstanding concern about American cyber capabilities.
episodes.why: Discovery pick — 80,000 Hours is a long-form interview show about tackling the world's biggest problems, new to this list; former NSC China director Julian Gewirtz explains that when Beijing warns of loss-of-control AI risks it means losing political control too, and what could actually shift its approach to safety.
